<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: equipment-purchase-planning.jpg | alt: "Business owner reviewing equipment purchase plans with financial advisor" | query: "business owner reviewing equipment investment plans" -->
## Proactive tax planning for equipment, inventory, and growth

Section 179 expensing, bonus depreciation, and cost segregation on a new facility are decisions that need to happen before you sign the purchase order, not after the fiscal year closes. Shawn T. Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc, holds the Certified Tax Coach credential specifically because standard tax prep does not go deep enough for a business buying equipment, carrying inventory, and running multiple entities at once.

Our team, including Chase Gubler, CPA, MAcc, and Peter Williams, EA, MAcc, meets with manufacturing and distribution clients on a quarterly cadence, not once a year. That means modeling the tax impact of a new production line before you finance it, timing inventory write-downs correctly, and structuring multi-entity operations, holding company, operating company, equipment leasing arm, so profits land where they are taxed most efficiently. Audit protection support backs every position we take, so you are covered if the IRS asks questions later.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: digital-accounting-portal.jpg | alt: "Laptop showing secure financial dashboard on a warehouse desk" | query: "laptop financial dashboard warehouse office" -->
## A modern, secure process that keeps you focused on production

Chasing paper invoices between the warehouse and the front office wastes time you do not have. Kinexus runs on a secure, cloud-based document portal, so purchase orders, vendor bills, and payroll records move digitally between your team and ours.

You get real-time financial dashboards instead of a shoebox handoff every quarter. Bank feeds sync automatically, documents are encrypted in transit and at rest, and your management team can pull a current P&L without waiting on a phone call. That leaves you free to manage production schedules and customer orders while the numbers stay current in the background.

### Physical therapy and professional practices
URL: /who-we-serve/physical-therapy-professional-services

<!-- block: hero-split | variant: image-right -->
## A CPA partner built for practice owners, not just providers

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: pt-clinic-owner-review.jpg | alt: "Physical therapy clinic owner reviewing financial reports with an accountant" | query: "physical therapist reviewing documents office" -->
Running a physical therapy clinic or professional practice means wearing two hats every day: clinician and business owner. Most general bookkeepers understand one side of that equation. Kinexus CPAs works with physical therapists, chiropractors, dentists, and other professional practices across St. George, UT, and we build our advice around the business decisions that come with running a licensed practice, not just the tax return that shows up once a year.

Shawn T. Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc, and the team at Kinexus have guided practice owners through staffing changes, equipment purchases, and growth decisions that a generic accountant would flag only after the fact. You need someone who already understands reimbursement cycles, contractor therapist arrangements, and the licensing costs baked into your industry. That's the starting point here, not an afterthought.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: pt-billing-cashflow.jpg | alt: "Front desk staff processing insurance billing paperwork at a therapy clinic" | query: "medical billing staff insurance paperwork" -->
## Financial challenges unique to physical therapy and professional practices

Practices like yours run into money problems that a restaurant or retail shop never sees. We hear the same issues from clinic owners across Washington County, and they usually fall into a few categories.

- Insurance reimbursement delays that create a gap between the visit and the deposit, sometimes 30 to 60 days out
- Payroll that mixes W-2 clinicians, 1099 contract therapists, and front-office staff, each with different tax treatment
- Equipment financing decisions for treatment tables, modalities, and build-outs that affect both cash flow and depreciation strategy
- Multi-location growth that multiplies bookkeeping, payroll runs, and state licensing compliance overnight
- Ongoing compliance costs tied to state licensing boards, HIPAA, and professional liability requirements

None of these are solved by tax software or a once-a-year filing appointment. They require someone watching the numbers between visits, not just at year-end.

<!-- block: service-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Accounting, tax, and payroll services tailored to your practice

We built our service lineup around how practices actually make and spend money, from insurance reimbursement timing to staffing mixes that change every quarter.

### Bookkeeping
icon: Receipt

Accurate, current books that reflect your real reimbursement timeline, not a guess based on deposits. We reconcile insurance payments, patient collections, and vendor bills so you know your true cash position every month, not just at tax time.

### Payroll
icon: Users

Payroll processing for W-2 clinicians and 1099 contract therapists alike, including salary changes, new hire setup, and filings handled correctly the first time. Fewer payroll corrections mean fewer awkward conversations with your staff.

### Business Tax Planning
icon: FileCheck

Year-round tax strategy for practices, not a single meeting in March. We plan around equipment purchases, entity structure, and owner compensation so your tax bill reflects decisions made in advance, not after the fact.

### Outsourced Accounting
icon: Building2

Full back-office support for practices that have outgrown a single bookkeeper but aren't ready for a full-time controller. You get monthly financials built for a healthcare or professional service business, delivered on a schedule you can plan around.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: pt-multi-location-growth.jpg | alt: "Business owners discussing expansion plans across multiple clinic locations" | query: "business owners planning expansion meeting" -->

Opening a second location, bringing on a partner, or restructuring ownership changes the math on everything from payroll taxes to liability exposure. Chase Gubler, CPA, MAcc, and RJ Mathews, CPA, work with practice owners on entity structuring decisions before those moves happen, not after a costly mistake shows up on a tax return.

Our Business Management Services translate your financials into the kind of strategic insight a CFO would deliver, at a fraction of the cost of hiring one full time. If you're weighing a partnership buy-in, a second clinic, or a new practice entity altogether, that's exactly the conversation this service is built for.

That means retirement plan structuring, entity election reviews, and quarterly check-ins designed to catch opportunities while there's still time to act, not a single rushed conversation every April. If your last CPA relationship consisted of dropping off a shoebox of receipts once a year, this is a different kind of engagement.

### Nonprofit organizations
URL: /who-we-serve/nonprofits

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## A CPA partner who understands nonprofit accounting

Running a nonprofit in Washington County means stretching every dollar toward mission, not overhead. Kinexus CPAs & Advisors works with local nonprofits on accounting, tax filings, and financial strategy built around fund accounting rules, not generic small-business bookkeeping repackaged for a 501(c)(3). Shawn T. Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc, and the team at Kinexus understand that a nonprofit's books answer to a board, a grantor, and the IRS all at once.

Most accounting firms treat nonprofit work as a side service. Kinexus treats it as a distinct discipline, with staff who know the difference between restricted and unrestricted funds and can explain that difference to a board member who isn't an accountant. That's the kind of clarity that keeps grant funding intact and audits uneventful.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: nonprofit-board-meeting-review.jpg | alt: "Nonprofit board members reviewing financial statements together at a table" | query: "nonprofit board meeting financial review" -->
## Challenges nonprofits face with limited financial resources

A lean nonprofit staff rarely includes a full-time controller, and that gap shows up fast. Grant reporting deadlines pile up, board members ask for financials in a format that actually makes sense, and someone still has to keep restricted and unrestricted funds separated correctly on paper, not just in spirit.

Common pressure points Kinexus sees among nonprofit clients in Washington County:

- Tracking multiple grants and donor restrictions without dedicated fund accounting software support
- Producing board-ready financial reports on a monthly or quarterly cadence
- Preparing for a financial statement audit required by a major grantor
- Managing payroll and benefits with one or two administrative staff wearing every hat
- Maintaining internal controls that satisfy both the board and outside auditors

An outsourced accounting relationship solves this without adding a full-time salary to the budget.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: nonprofit-fund-accounting-review.jpg | alt: "Accountant reviewing grant and donation records on a laptop" | query: "accountant reviewing grant financial records" -->
## Bookkeeping and accounting built for fund accounting needs

Donor dollars come with conditions, and a general ledger built for a retail shop won't track them correctly. Kinexus sets up bookkeeping and outsourced accounting around program-based and grant-based reporting, so a director can tell a funder exactly how their money was spent, down to the program line item.

Monthly close, expense classification, and reconciliation happen through a modern, secure digital process, which means board treasurers get clean statements without chasing down a shoebox of receipts. RJ Mathews, CPA, and Morgan Nethercott, CPA, both work directly with clients who need audit-ready books, not just a checkbook register that balances.

The result is transparency a board can stand behind and a paper trail that holds up when a grantor or auditor asks questions.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: nonprofit-tax-exempt-filing.jpg | alt: "Tax preparer reviewing IRS Form 990 documents for a nonprofit client" | query: "tax preparer reviewing nonprofit tax forms" -->
## Form 990 preparation and nonprofit tax compliance

Losing tax-exempt status over a missed or mishandled Form 990 is a real risk, not a hypothetical one. Kinexus prepares Form 990, 990-EZ, and 990-T filings with attention to the disclosures that protect exempt status, including unrelated business income, executive compensation reporting, and public support test calculations that keep a public charity classified correctly.

This isn't a once-a-year filing errand. Andy Stewart, EA, and Peter Williams, EA, MAcc, monitor compliance changes throughout the year so a nonprofit isn't caught off guard by a new reporting threshold or a state registration renewal. That proactive approach matters more for nonprofits than most businesses, since a compliance misstep can threaten the exemption itself. For organizations facing an IRS notice or inquiry, Kinexus also provides [audit protection](/what-we-do/audit-protection) and [IRS representation](/services/irs-representation-tax-resolution) support.

<!-- block: feature-grid | variant: 3-col -->

Executive directors didn't take the job to process payroll or reconcile a credit card statement. Kinexus handles the back office so nonprofit staff can spend their hours on programs and donors instead of paperwork.

### Payroll Processing
icon: Clock

Accurate, on-time payroll for staff, including tax filings, benefits deductions, and W-2 preparation, run through the same secure digital platform used for accounting.

### Administrative Back-Office Support
icon: Users

Bill payment, invoicing, and expense tracking handled consistently, freeing a small staff from tasks that eat into program hours every week.

### Grant and Donor Reporting Prep
icon: FileText

Financial data organized and formatted so grant reports and donor statements go out accurate and on schedule, without a last-minute scramble.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: nonprofit-executive-director-planning.jpg | alt: "Executive director and advisor discussing a nonprofit budget forecast" | query: "executive director advisor budget meeting" -->
## CFO-level guidance for growing nonprofit organizations

A nonprofit that's outgrown its founding budget needs more than compliance work. It needs someone who can translate financial statements into a decision about whether to apply for a new grant, hire a program manager, or hold off another year. That's what Business Management Services is built for.

Chase Gubler, CPA, MAcc, works with executive directors and boards on budgeting, cash flow forecasting, and sustainability planning tied directly to grant cycles and fundraising calendars. Instead of reviewing financials once a year at the annual meeting, boards get ongoing insight into where the organization stands and what decisions are coming next quarter, not just what already happened last quarter.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: nonprofit-consultation-meeting.jpg | alt: "Nonprofit leader shaking hands with a financial advisor in an office" | query: "nonprofit leader advisor handshake meeting" -->

Whether the immediate need is a clean Form 990, a board report that finally makes sense, or a second set of eyes before an audit, Kinexus CPAs & Advisors works with nonprofit leaders across St. George and Washington County on exactly these problems. Schedule a consultation and talk through what your organization needs this fiscal year.

## Who we are

### Our team
URL: /who-we-are/team

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## A dedicated partner behind every client relationship

Most CPA firms meet you once a year, hand you a return, and disappear until next April. That's not how Kinexus works. Every credentialed advisor on this team, from the CPAs who structure your entity to the Enrolled Agents who stand between you and the IRS, treats tax and accounting as a year-round conversation, not a once-a-year transaction.

We're based in St. George, and we built this team around the businesses that actually operate here: contractors pouring foundations in Washington County, restaurant owners managing food costs on Main Street, real estate investors closing on rentals across southern Utah, and medical practices trying to keep more of what they bill. Here's who you'll be working with.

<!-- block: team-grid | variant: 2-col -->
## Leadership and advisory team

### Shawn T. Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc
Founding Partner

Shawn holds a CPA license, a Master of Accounting, and a Certified Tax Coach (CTC) designation, a credential fewer than a few thousand advisors nationwide carry because it requires ongoing training specifically in proactive tax reduction strategy. That's the lens he brings to every engagement: not how to file a return correctly, but how to structure a business so the tax bill is smaller before the year even ends. He works closely with construction and real estate clients, where entity structure and timing decisions carry outsized tax consequences.

### RJ Mathews, CPA
Partner

RJ focuses on the advisory side of the practice, translating financial statements into decisions business owners can actually act on. Restaurant and service-based business clients rely on him for margin analysis, cash flow forecasting, and the kind of month-over-month guidance that keeps a growing business from outrunning its own books.

### Chase Gubler, CPA, MAcc
Partner

Chase pairs his CPA license with a Master of Accounting and works primarily with entrepreneurs launching new ventures and established businesses scaling into their next phase. He's often the first call for clients weighing entity structure, growth financing, or an acquisition.

### Morgan Nethercott, CPA
Partner

Morgan leads client engagements in medical and professional practices, where compliance complexity and staffing costs demand a CPA who understands the operational side of running a practice, not just the tax side of owning one.

<!-- block: team-grid | variant: 2-col -->
## Tax strategy and resolution specialists

### Andrew Stewart, EA
Enrolled Agent

Known around the office as Andy, Andrew holds the Enrolled Agent (EA) credential, which grants him unlimited rights to represent clients directly before the IRS. When a client receives a notice, gets flagged for an audit, or needs someone to negotiate a resolution on their behalf, Andy is the specialist handling it, backed by the firm's Audit Protection service.

### Peter Williams, EA, MAcc
Enrolled Agent

Peter combines his EA credential with a Master of Accounting, giving him both the representation authority to deal with the IRS and the technical depth to build multi-year tax strategies for growing businesses. He works alongside Shawn on advanced planning engagements where entity choice, retirement contributions, and depreciation strategy intersect.

Between Andy, Peter, and Shawn's Certified Tax Coach credential, clients get a planning team built for two jobs most firms treat separately: keeping the tax bill low all year, and having someone qualified to fight for you if the IRS ever sends a letter.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: bookkeeping-specialist-office.jpg | alt: "Bookkeeping specialist working at a computer with financial software open" | query: "bookkeeper working office computer" -->
## Accounting, bookkeeping, and payroll specialists

Behind every CPA and EA at Kinexus is a team that handles the daily mechanics: transaction coding, bill pay, invoicing, and payroll runs that have to land on time, every time. Leslye Haws, one of the firm's bookkeeping specialists, is the person many clients talk to most often, because she's the one keeping their books current between the quarterly planning calls.

This team runs on the same modern, secure digital process the rest of the firm uses: cloud-based accounting platforms, encrypted document portals, and payroll systems that handle employee setup and salary changes without a stack of paper. It's a quieter job than tax strategy, but it's the reason the numbers your CPA advises on are actually accurate.

## Popular guidance for growing businesses

A few articles keep coming up in client conversations regardless of what page of the archive they're buried on. Start here if you're not sure where else to look.

### Is your business structure costing you money
photo: business-structure-review.jpg
query: business owner reviewing legal documents office

Entity choice affects self-employment tax, liability exposure, and how much you keep at year-end. This piece covers the signals that it's time to revisit your LLC, S-corp, or partnership setup. [Read more](/is-your-business-structure-costing-you-money)

### When and why every business owner needs a business valuation
photo: business-valuation-meeting.jpg
query: accountant presenting financial report chart

A valuation matters for more than a sale. Owners planning a buyout, financing round, or estate transfer need a defensible number, and this article explains when to get one done. [Read more](/when-and-why-every-business-owner-needs-a-business-valuation)

### Zero-based budgeting for persistent inflation
photo: budgeting-review-laptop.jpg
query: small business owner budgeting laptop

## Popular topics in tax planning and business advisory

A handful of themes keep showing up across this archive, and for good reason. Business owners in Washington County are asking the same core questions: is my entity structure still the right one, is my back office keeping pace with growth, and am I planning for taxes year-round instead of scrambling every April.

Entity structuring is one of the most-read topics here, and it's easy to see why. A structure that made sense at $200,000 in revenue can cost real money at $2 million. Our piece on [whether your business structure is costing you money](/is-your-business-structure-costing-you-money) walks through the warning signs.

Operational efficiency is the other recurring thread. Owners want fewer surprises in their books and a clearer read on margin. Articles on [zero-based budgeting during persistent inflation](/zero-based-budgeting-a-smarter-way-to-manage-your-money-during-persistent-inflation) and [upskilling a workforce facing labor shortages](/upskilling-your-workforce-a-smart-strategy-for-overcoming-labor-market-shortages) both tackle that from different angles. If you want the full picture rather than a single post, the [insights hub](/resources/insights) organizes everything by category.

## Stay ahead with year-round tax planning updates

A lot of these posts exist because once-a-year tax prep leaves too much on the table. Deadlines for quarterly estimates, entity elections, and depreciation decisions happen throughout the year, and by the time an April filing rolls around, most of the useful decisions have already passed.

That's the thinking behind this blog and behind how Kinexus works with clients generally. Shawn T. Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc, RJ Mathews, CPA, and the rest of the team treat tax planning as a running conversation, checking in on numbers as they change rather than reconstructing a year after the fact. Reading through past posts is a reasonable way to get a feel for how that ongoing relationship actually works before you ever pick up the phone.

## Why our team writes about proactive tax and business strategy

Most accounting content online is written to fill a keyword quota. Ours isn't. Shawn Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc, and the rest of the Kinexus team write about the same issues we're actively solving for clients: WIP schedule accuracy for a Washington County contractor, entity structuring for a new restaurant group, quarterly estimates for a physician moving from W-2 to 1099 income.

We don't believe tax work should happen once a year in March. Planning happens in July, October, and January, whenever a decision actually changes the outcome. That's the philosophy behind every post here: fewer surprises, more decisions made with real numbers in hand. If a topic reads like it came from a CFO conversation rather than a tax prep checklist, that's intentional.

## Stay ahead with proactive tax and financial strategy

Most CPA firms show up once a year, hand you a return, and disappear until next April. Kinexus CPAs works differently. Shawn T. Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc, and the rest of the team meet with clients throughout the year, because a tax strategy decided in March is worth more than one decided in April.

That's the thread running through this archive. A WIP schedule review in June affects your bonding capacity in December. An entity structure conversation before you sign a lease changes your tax bill for years. Wait until the deadline, and the best options are already off the table.

Construction firms, restaurant groups, real estate investors, medical practices, and service businesses across St George, UT face the same problem: money moves faster than annual meetings can track. That's why this archive exists, and why Kinexus builds client relationships around ongoing planning instead of one appointment a year.

## Why proactive planning beats year-end scrambling

Most of what ends up in a January scramble was visible back in July. A revenue jump, a new hire, an equipment purchase, a rental property closing, each one shifts a tax picture that gets expensive to fix after December 31. Shawn T. Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc, built the firm's advisory model around quarterly check-ins instead of a single annual meeting, because tax law rewards decisions made before the year closes, not after. Chase Gubler, CPA, MAcc, and Morgan Nethercott, CPA, work the same way with clients across construction, restaurants, real estate, and professional services: watch the numbers monthly, flag what matters, and put it in front of the client while there's still time to act. A return filed in April tells you what already happened. A conversation held in September changes what happens next. That gap between preparation and planning is where most of the savings live.

<!-- block: form | variant: newsletter -->
## Stay ahead with tax strategy updates

Tax law changes more than once a year, and most of the updates that matter never make the evening news. Sign up to get planning alerts, deadline reminders, and industry-specific tips sent directly, the kind of information Shawn Gubler and the Kinexus team already share with clients during quarterly reviews. No spam, no filler, just the items worth acting on before they cost you money.

### Selling a business rental or large asset this year call your cpa before you sign
URL: /selling-a-business-rental-or-large-asset-this-year-call-your-cpa-before-you-sign

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Why timing matters before you sign anything

Once a purchase agreement is signed, most of your tax-saving options disappear with it. The sale price is locked, the structure is set, and the IRS treats the transaction as final from that date forward. Business owners across St. George, Washington County, and southern Utah call us every year after they've already accepted an offer, hoping we can soften the tax hit after the fact. Sometimes we can help. Often, the best moves, like restructuring the sale as an asset purchase instead of a stock sale, or timing the closing to land in a lower-income year, were only available before ink hit paper.

Selling a business, a rental property, or a piece of major equipment is one of the biggest financial events a business owner will face. A short conversation with your CPA before you sign preserves options that disappear the moment a deal closes. That's the entire premise behind this page, and it's worth taking seriously before your next big sale.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: business-sale-tax-planning-meeting.jpg | alt: "Business owner and CPA reviewing sale documents at a desk" | query: "business owner accountant meeting documents" -->
## Tax consequences of selling a business

How you sell a business changes what you owe almost as much as how much you sell it for. An asset sale and an entity (stock) sale are taxed differently, and buyers and sellers often prefer opposite structures for opposite reasons. Sellers frequently favor a stock sale because gains are taxed at capital gains rates. Buyers usually want an asset sale so they can step up basis and depreciate assets going forward. Whoever negotiates that point without a CPA at the table tends to give up value they didn't know was on the table.

Depreciation recapture is the other piece owners miss. If you've written off equipment, leasehold improvements, or vehicles over the years, part of that gain on sale gets taxed as ordinary income, not capital gains, no matter how the deal is structured. Shawn T. Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc, works through these scenarios with business owners before a letter of intent is even drafted, modeling the tax difference between structures so the number on the settlement statement doesn't surprise anyone. Our [business tax](/what-we-do/business-tax) and [advanced tax planning](/services/advanced-tax-planning) work exists specifically for moments like this.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: rental-property-investor-review.jpg | alt: "Real estate investor reviewing property documents with financial advisor" | query: "real estate investor reviewing documents" -->
## What to know before selling a rental or investment property

Real estate investors and landlords have more planning tools available than most sellers realize, but nearly all of them require action before closing.

- **1031 exchanges**, Deferring capital gains by rolling proceeds into another investment property requires a qualified intermediary lined up and a 45-day identification clock that starts at closing, not after.
- **Depreciation recapture**, Every year of depreciation taken on a rental comes back as taxable income at sale, taxed at rates up to 25 percent, regardless of how long you held the property.
- **Installment sales**, Spreading the gain over multiple tax years through seller financing can keep you out of a higher bracket, but the note terms have to be drafted correctly from day one.
- **Cost segregation history**, If you've accelerated depreciation on the property, that acceleration affects both your recapture exposure and your exchange math.

Generalist accounting firms handle a rental sale a few times a year. Real estate is one of our core niches at Kinexus, and our team works with investors and landlords across St. George on exactly these decisions through [real estate investor advisory](/who-we-serve/real-estate-investors) and [real estate](/who-we-serve/real-estate) planning, before the purchase and sale agreement is final, not after.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: construction-equipment-sale-review.jpg | alt: "Contractor reviewing equipment sale paperwork on a job site" | query: "contractor reviewing paperwork equipment" -->
## Large asset sales and equipment disposals

Selling a piece of heavy equipment, a company vehicle, or a medical practice's imaging equipment triggers the same recapture math as selling a building, just on a smaller scale. Contractors who sold a truck or excavator after taking Section 179 or bonus depreciation often owe more in tax on that single sale than they expected, because the deduction they took years ago comes due all at once. Medical professionals selling practice equipment or a service business owner unloading office assets face the identical issue.

The fix usually isn't complicated, but it has to happen before the sale, not on next April's return. Timing the sale to offset against a loss year, pairing it with a new equipment purchase, or spreading multiple asset sales across two tax years are all options while the deal is still being negotiated. Peter Williams, EA, MAcc, and Andy Stewart, EA, regularly walk construction and medical clients through these calculations before assets change hands, using the industry context built through our [construction](/who-we-serve/construction) and [medical professionals](/who-we-serve/medical-professionals) advisory work.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## How proactive tax planning changes the outcome

Most CPA relationships run on a once-a-year cycle: gather documents in March, file by April, talk again next year. That rhythm works fine for a routine return. It fails completely for a business sale, a rental disposal, or an equipment sell-off, because by the time those documents land on a desk in tax season, the transaction closed months earlier and the structure is locked.

Kinexus runs on a different model. Year-round tax planning means the conversation about selling your rental, your business, or your excavator happens while you're still weighing offers, not after you've accepted one. That's when entity restructuring, installment sale terms, 1031 timelines, and multi-year gain spreading are still live options. Chase Gubler, CPA, MAcc, and Morgan Nethercott, CPA, build these scenarios into ongoing client relationships, not one-off engagements, so the planning is already in motion when an offer shows up. If your current setup is working against you, it's also worth reading [is your business structure costing you money](/is-your-business-structure-costing-you-money) and [when and why every business owner needs a business valuation](/when-and-why-every-business-owner-needs-a-business-valuation) before you list anything for sale.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: cpa-consultation-handshake.jpg | alt: "CPA and business owner shaking hands after a planning consultation" | query: "business handshake professional consultation" -->
## Talk to your CPA before you sign

If a sale, a rental disposal, or a major asset transfer is anywhere on your calendar this year, the highest-value phone call you can make is the one before the paperwork, not after. Once the agreement is signed, the tax outcome is mostly set. Before that point, there's still room to structure the deal, time the closing, or line up a 1031 exchange that saves real money.

Kinexus CPAs & Advisors works with contractors, restaurant operators, real estate investors, medical professionals, and service-based business owners across St. George, UT on exactly these decisions, backed by CPAs, an EA, and a CTC-credentialed tax strategist on staff. Schedule a consultation before you sign anything, and let's model the numbers together.

### When and why every business owner needs a business valuation
URL: /when-and-why-every-business-owner-needs-a-business-valuation

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: left-aligned -->
## Why the number in your head isn't a real valuation

Most business owners can rattle off a number when asked what their company is worth. Usually it's built from a competitor's sale price, a comment a banker made in passing, or a multiple pulled from an industry rumor. None of that holds up when it actually matters.

A real valuation is built on methodology: adjusted financials, industry benchmarks, cash flow analysis, and defensible assumptions a lender, buyer, or court will accept. The gut-feel number and the defensible number are often nowhere close, and the gap shows up at the worst possible time, mid-negotiation, mid-divorce, or mid-financing application. If you're making a decision that hinges on what your business is worth, guessing is a risk you don't need to take.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: business-owner-reviewing-documents.jpg | alt: "Business owner reviewing financial documents with a CPA advisor" | query: "business owner meeting with accountant" -->
## Key moments that trigger the need for a valuation

A formal valuation isn't something you need every year, but there are specific moments where operating without one becomes expensive. Owners typically reach out to Kinexus for a valuation ahead of one of these events:

- Selling the business, merging with another company, or fielding an unsolicited offer
- Bringing on new partners, shareholders, or an ESOP
- Divorce or estate planning where the business is a marital or estate asset
- Drafting or updating a buy-sell agreement between co-owners
- Applying for financing or an SBA loan that requires a documented valuation
- Litigation, shareholder disputes, or IRS matters that require a defensible number

Each of these situations puts real money on the table, and each one is judged by a bank, a court, an ex-spouse's attorney, or a business partner who has no reason to accept your estimate at face value. A CPA-prepared valuation gives you a number that stands up to scrutiny instead of one that starts an argument.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: cfo-advisory-meeting.jpg | alt: "CPA and business owner discussing growth strategy at a desk" | query: "CFO advisor discussing business strategy" -->
## How proactive valuation supports growth planning, not just transactions

Most firms only bring up valuation when a sale is already on the table. That's backwards. By the time a deal is in motion, there's little room left to improve the number.

Kinexus treats valuation as part of ongoing business management services, the same CFO-level advisory work that tracks your margins, tax position, and entity structure year-round. Knowing what your business is worth today, and what's actually driving or dragging that number, shapes decisions long before a sale: how you price a job, whether to add a location, when to bring on a partner, or how to structure a buy-sell agreement before it's needed. Owners who understand their valuation trajectory make better decisions at every stage, not just the exit. That's a different conversation than a once-a-year tax appointment, and it's the one worth having.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## What goes into an accurate business valuation

A credible valuation pulls from more than a tax return. It starts with normalized financial statements, adjusting for owner compensation, one-time expenses, and related-party transactions that distort the real picture. From there, we look at industry benchmarks and comparable transactions to see how similar businesses have actually sold, not what a rule-of-thumb multiple suggests.

Cash flow gets weighted heavily, since most valuation methods (income, market, or asset-based) ultimately come back to what the business can reliably generate going forward. Tangible and intangible assets, equipment, real estate, customer contracts, goodwill, get accounted for separately. Current market conditions, financing rates, and buyer appetite in your specific sector round out the picture. None of this is guesswork; it's a documented process that produces a number you can defend to a bank, a buyer, or a judge.

<!-- block: industry-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Industry-specific considerations for valuation

A generic valuation approach misses what actually drives value in your industry. Kinexus applies methodology built around how each sector operates.

### Construction
icon: Hammer

Work-in-progress schedules, bonding capacity, and backlog value matter as much as trailing revenue. A contractor's valuation has to account for percentage-of-completion accounting and equipment depreciation.

### Restaurants
icon: Building

Multi-location operators face franchise agreements, lease terms, and labor cost ratios that swing value significantly. Same-store sales trends carry more weight than total revenue alone.

### Medical Professionals
icon: Stethoscope

Practice valuations weigh payer mix, provider-dependent goodwill, and equipment age. A physician-owned practice with heavy owner dependency values differently than a group practice with associate providers.

### Real Estate
icon: Building2

Investment portfolios and rental operations are valued on cash-on-cash return, cap rates, and debt structure, not just assessed property value.

### Service-Based Businesses
icon: Briefcase

Consultants, agencies, and staffing firms are judged on client concentration, recurring revenue, and how much of the business depends on the owner personally.

<!-- block: process-steps | variant: horizontal -->
## How Kinexus guides you through the valuation process

### Understand the reason behind the number
We start by identifying why you need the valuation, sale, financing, buy-sell agreement, or litigation, since the purpose shapes the methodology.

### Gather financials digitally
Documents come to us through a secure, modern client portal, no paper files, no in-person drop-offs required.

### Apply industry-specific methodology
Shawn T. Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc, and the team apply benchmarks and adjustments specific to construction, restaurants, real estate, medical, or service-based businesses.

### Review findings together
You get a plain-language walkthrough of the number and what's driving it, not just a report to file away.

### Fold it into ongoing planning
The valuation feeds directly into tax planning, entity structuring, and growth strategy conversations going forward.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: st-george-business-owner-handshake.jpg | alt: "Business owner and CPA advisor shaking hands after a meeting" | query: "business owner advisor handshake office" -->
## Get clarity on what your business is worth

Whether you're planning a sale, adding a partner, or just tired of guessing, a defensible valuation puts real numbers behind the decision. Kinexus CPAs & Advisors works with contractors, restaurant operators, medical practices, real estate investors, and service-based businesses across St. George, UT on exactly this kind of work.

### Transfer pricing and related entities what business owners need to know
URL: /transfer-pricing-and-related-entities-what-business-owners-need-to-know

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## What transfer pricing means for multi-entity businesses

Transfer pricing sounds like something that only applies to multinational corporations shifting profits between countries. It doesn't. Any time two businesses under common ownership exchange goods, services, rent, or cash, the IRS treats that exchange as a related-party transaction, and the price attached to it has to hold up the same way a deal between strangers would.

That covers more situations than most owners realize. A contractor who runs the operating company through one LLC and holds the equipment or the job site property in another is dealing with transfer pricing. So is a physician whose practice entity pays rent to a separate real estate holding company, or a restaurant group with a management entity charging fees to three locations. The IRS calls this the arm's-length standard: related entities have to price their internal transactions as if they were unrelated parties negotiating in the open market. Get it wrong, even without intent, and the exposure lands on the tax return, not the org chart.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: intercompany-transaction-review.jpg | alt: "Business owner reviewing intercompany invoices and financial statements at a desk" | query: "business owner reviewing financial documents office" -->
## When related-entity transactions trigger IRS scrutiny

Certain patterns catch attention faster than others. Management fees paid from an operating company to a holding entity are common in construction and multi-location restaurant groups, and examiners look closely at whether the fee reflects real services at a market rate or simply moves income to a lower-taxed entity. Rent charged from a property-holding LLC to the operating business is another frequent flag, especially when the rent doesn't match comparable local lease rates in St George or Washington County.

Intercompany loans raise similar questions. If one entity lends money to a related business without a written note, a market interest rate, and a repayment schedule, the IRS can recharacterize the loan as a disguised distribution or dividend. Real estate investors who move cash between rental entities, and medical practices that split the clinical and real estate sides of the business, run into this constantly. None of these structures are wrong. They just need pricing that a stranger would have agreed to.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: audit-notice-review.jpg | alt: "CPA reviewing an IRS notice letter with a client" | query: "accountant reviewing document client meeting" -->
## Risks of getting related-entity pricing wrong

When the IRS decides a related-party price wasn't at arm's length, it doesn't just ask for an adjustment. It reallocates income between the entities under IRC Section 482, which can trigger:

- Back taxes on income shifted to the entity that should have reported it
- Accuracy-related penalties on top of the reallocated amount
- Interest that compounds from the original filing date, not the audit date
- A wider audit scope, since one flagged transaction often leads examiners to review every related-entity transfer
- Higher future audit risk once a business has an adjustment on record

Our enrolled agents, Andy Stewart, EA, and Peter Williams, EA, MAcc, handle audit protection and IRS representation cases where related-entity pricing is the core issue. The pattern is consistent: the businesses that get flagged usually had a reasonable structure, just no documentation to support it. That gap is what turns a routine notice into a multi-year exam.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: entity-structure-planning-meeting.jpg | alt: "Accountant and business owner discussing entity structure documents at a table" | query: "accountant client meeting planning documents" -->
## How growing businesses structure multi-entity transactions correctly

Correct transfer pricing starts with documentation, not spreadsheets after the fact. Every intercompany transaction, a management fee, rent, a loan, needs a written agreement, a defensible method for setting the price, and evidence that the method reflects market terms. For rent, that usually means a comparison to lease rates for similar space in the same market. For management fees, it means documenting the actual services performed and benchmarking the fee against what an unrelated provider would charge.

Shawn Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc, and Chase Gubler, CPA, MAcc, work with construction groups, real estate investors, and multi-entity medical practices to set up this documentation before the entities start transacting, not after a notice arrives. That often overlaps with [entity structuring](/services/entity-structuring) work: deciding which activities belong in which entity, how they should be capitalized, and how the intercompany agreements between them need to read. Businesses that get this right treat it as infrastructure, the same way they'd treat a chart of accounts or a payroll system.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Why proactive planning beats after-the-fact fixes

Most transfer pricing problems don't start as tax problems. They start as operational decisions, an owner sets up a second LLC to hold real estate, or splits a practice into a clinical entity and a management entity, and nobody prices the transactions between them until the accountant asks during tax prep. By then the pattern is already on prior returns.

Year-round tax planning catches this before it compounds. Reviewing intercompany transactions as part of ongoing [advanced tax planning](/services/advanced-tax-planning), rather than once during filing season, means pricing gets set with intention and documented in real time. For construction companies with equipment-holding entities, restaurant groups with management companies, and real estate investors running multiple rental LLCs, that difference shows up the first time the IRS asks a question, not the first time a return gets filed.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: multi-entity-consultation.jpg | alt: "Business owner and CPA shaking hands after a planning consultation" | query: "business handshake professional consultation office" -->
## Get a review of your entity structure and related-party transactions

If your business runs through more than one entity, whether that's a holding company and an operating company, sister businesses under common ownership, or a practice split between clinical and real estate sides, it's worth a direct look at how those entities price transactions with each other. Kinexus CPAs works with contractors, restaurant groups, real estate investors, and medical practices across St George on exactly this kind of multi-entity structure.

Schedule a consultation to review your entity structure and intercompany transactions before they become an audit question instead of a planning conversation.

[Schedule a consultation](/contact)

### Is your business structure costing you money
URL: /is-your-business-structure-costing-you-money

## How entity choice quietly drains business profits

Most business owners pick a structure once, usually in the first year, and never look at it again. A sole proprietorship or single-member LLC felt right when the business was small. Five years and a lot more revenue later, that same structure can be quietly costing thousands of dollars a year.

Here's the mechanism: sole proprietors and default LLCs pay self-employment tax, 15.3%, on every dollar of net profit. An S-corp election lets an owner split income between a reasonable salary and distributions, and distributions aren't subject to that tax. On top of the tax gap, an outdated structure can leave real estate, equipment, or personal assets exposed to business liability that a properly layered entity setup would have shielded.

We see this most often with contractors who started as a one-person LLC and now run crews on multiple job sites, and with service businesses that scaled past six figures without ever revisiting the paperwork filed at formation. The structure that made sense at $80,000 in revenue rarely makes sense at $400,000.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Signs your current structure no longer fits your business

A structure review isn't something to schedule only when the IRS sends a letter. Certain milestones are reliable signals that the entity on file no longer matches the business actually running.

- Net income has climbed past $60,000 to $80,000 and self-employment tax is now a real line item
- You've brought on a partner, co-owner, or investor and profit-sharing needs formal documentation
- You're operating in more than one location, such as a second restaurant site or a new service territory
- You've purchased rental property or a commercial building and it's titled under your operating business
- You've hired W-2 employees and payroll, workers' comp, and liability exposure have all increased
- You're a physician, dentist, or healthcare provider adding a second practice location or bringing on associates
- You're holding multiple rental properties, flips, or a mix of long-term and short-term rentals under one LLC

Any one of these on its own is worth a conversation. Two or three together usually mean money is being left on the table right now.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: business-structure-review-meeting.jpg | alt: "Business owner reviewing entity structure documents with a CPA" | query: "business owner reviewing documents with advisor" -->
## What a structure review with Kinexus involves

A structure review at Kinexus starts with your actual tax return, not a generic checklist. We compare what you're paying under your current setup against what an S-corp election, a multi-entity structure, or a holding company arrangement would produce over the next twelve months, then walk through the tradeoffs in plain terms.

Shawn T. Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc, and Chase Gubler, CPA, MAcc, lead this analysis with a Master of Accounting-level view of how entity choice interacts with self-employment tax, retirement contributions, and multi-state exposure for owners who operate across Utah and beyond. For businesses that have grown into real estate holdings, multiple locations, or a mix of active and passive income, we model multi-entity or holding company setups rather than treating structure as a one-size-fits-all decision.

This isn't a once-a-year exercise. It plugs directly into [year-round business tax planning](/what-we-do/business-tax) and [advanced tax strategy work](/services/advanced-tax-planning), so the structure gets revisited as revenue, staffing, and asset holdings change, not just when a return is due.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: cpa-entity-structuring-consultation.jpg | alt: "CPA and business owner discussing entity structuring options on a laptop" | query: "accountant client consultation laptop office" -->
## Common restructuring scenarios for St. George business owners

### LLC electing S-corp status
icon: DollarSign

A construction or service-based LLC that's clearing $90,000 or more in net profit often elects S-corp taxation, sets a reasonable owner salary, and takes remaining profit as distributions not subject to self-employment tax. For an owner in that range, the annual tax savings can run into the thousands.

### Real estate investor separating properties
icon: Home

An investor holding four rental properties in a single LLC carries liability risk across all four if one tenant sues. Splitting properties into separate entities, sometimes under a parent holding company, isolates risk property by property. [Real estate investors](/who-we-serve/real-estate-investors) with growing portfolios are the clearest case for this move.

### Entrepreneur scaling into a holding company
icon: Building2

An entrepreneur running two or three related businesses, say a service company and a real estate arm holding the building it operates from, often benefits from a holding structure that centralizes ownership, simplifies financing conversations, and cleans up the balance sheet for a future sale.

<!-- block: feature-grid | variant: 3-col -->
## Why timing matters for restructuring decisions

An S-corp election has a filing deadline, generally 75 days into the tax year it's meant to cover. Miss that window and the savings wait another twelve months. The same is true for setting up new entities before a property closing, before a new partner buys in, or before year-end. Structure and entity paperwork filed in January doesn't retroactively apply to income already earned in November.

Waiting until tax season to ask "should my structure be different" almost always means losing a full year of savings that a review in Q3 or Q4 would have captured. Proactive timing is the difference between planning and reacting.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Get a clear answer about your business structure

If you've been operating the same LLC or sole proprietorship since you started and revenue, staff, or property holdings have grown since then, it's worth twenty minutes to find out whether that structure still serves you. Kinexus CPAs & Advisors works with contractors, restaurant operators, real estate investors, medical practices, and service businesses across St. George through a secure, digital process for document review and filing, so a structure analysis doesn't mean a stack of paperwork on your desk.

Schedule a consultation and bring your last return. We'll tell you plainly whether your current entity is costing you money and what changing it would actually look like.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: st-george-business-owner-consultation.jpg | alt: "Small business owner shaking hands with a CPA advisor in a modern office" | query: "business owner handshake advisor office" -->
## Schedule a consultation

### Zero based budgeting a smarter way to manage your money during persistent inflation
URL: /zero-based-budgeting-a-smarter-way-to-manage-your-money-during-persistent-inflation

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: rising-costs-budget-review.jpg | alt: "Business owner reviewing rising costs on a laptop and printed spreadsheet" | query: "small business owner reviewing financial documents" -->
## Why traditional budgets break down when prices keep rising

Most budgets get built once a year and then coast on autopilot. You take last year's numbers, add three or five percent for inflation, and call it done. That worked fine when costs moved slowly and predictably. It doesn't work now.

Material costs for a St. George contractor can jump mid-project. A restaurant's food cost percentage can swing month to month based on produce and protein pricing alone. A service business watching software subscriptions and contractor rates creep upward needs a budget that reflects this month's reality, not last January's assumptions. A static, percentage-based plan quietly falls out of sync with actual spending, and by the time the gap shows up on a profit and loss statement, margin is already gone. Businesses in Washington County need a budgeting method built to move as fast as costs do.

<!-- block: content-prose -->
## Every dollar gets assigned a job before the month starts

Zero based budgeting flips the traditional model. Instead of starting from last period's numbers and adjusting up or down, every budget period starts at zero. Every dollar of expected income gets assigned a specific purpose, and every expense line has to be justified again from scratch rather than automatically carried forward.

That means payroll, materials, rent, software, marketing, and everything else get re-evaluated each cycle instead of rubber-stamped. If a line item no longer earns its place, it gets cut or reduced. If a cost has grown, that growth gets addressed immediately instead of discovered three months later during tax prep.

The method takes more discipline upfront than a rollover budget. It also produces a document that actually matches what's happening in the business right now, which matters most when supplier pricing, wage rates, and interest costs are all moving at once.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: contractor-reviewing-budget.jpg | alt: "Contractor reviewing a job cost budget on a tablet at a worksite" | query: "contractor reviewing paperwork jobsite" -->
## How this approach protects margins for small business owners

Inflation doesn't hit every business the same way, but it hits every business somewhere. Zero based budgeting forces that impact into view before it erodes profit.

- A contractor tracking a job cost line every month catches material overruns while there's still time to adjust a bid or renegotiate a subcontractor rate, rather than finding out at project close.
- A restaurant operator justifying food and labor costs each period spots supplier price increases immediately and can adjust menu pricing or portion controls before margin slips.
- A service business reviewing every software subscription, contractor fee, and marketing line each month cuts spend that no longer produces a return, instead of paying for it out of habit.
- Owners across construction, restaurants, and service industries get an early warning system for cost creep instead of a year-end surprise.

This is the difference between reacting to a bad quarter and preventing one. Kinexus CPAs works with construction, restaurant, and service-based clients across St. George who use this exact discipline to keep margin intact when input costs move without warning.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: cpa-tax-planning-meeting.jpg | alt: "CPA and small business client reviewing tax planning documents together at a desk" | query: "accountant client tax planning meeting" -->
## Where zero based budgeting fits alongside proactive tax planning

A zero based budget is a planning tool. On its own, it tells you where money should go. Paired with year-round tax planning, it tells you what those decisions actually cost or save you at filing time, which is where most generic budgeting advice stops short.

When every expense line is justified monthly instead of guessed at annually, the numbers feeding your tax strategy get sharper. Equipment purchases, owner compensation, retirement contributions, and entity structure decisions all work better when they're based on current, granular data rather than a rough annual estimate pulled together in March.

This is the model Kinexus CPAs builds advisory work around: proactive, year-round business tax planning that uses real-time financial detail instead of once-a-year reconciliation. Shawn T. Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc, and the firm's team of CPAs and enrolled agents connect budgeting discipline directly to tax strategy and cash flow decisions, not as a separate exercise handled by a different advisor at a different time of year.

<!-- block: process-steps | variant: horizontal -->
## Getting started without overhauling your entire accounting system

You don't need to rebuild your books to try this. Zero based budgeting works as a targeted exercise before it becomes a company-wide standard.

### Pick one category or department

Start with the expense area causing the most stress right now, whether that's materials, food cost, payroll, or software spend, and rebuild that single budget from zero for one period.

### Justify every line for that period

Work through each expense in the chosen category and require a reason for it to exist this month, not just a history of existing last month.

### Review results and expand

Compare the rebuilt category against the old rollover version, measure the difference, and use that result to decide whether to extend the method to other parts of the budget.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: st-george-business-consultation.jpg | alt: "St. George business owner meeting with a CPA advisor in an office setting" | query: "business consultation office meeting" -->
## Build a budget that works with a St. George advisory team

Zero based budgeting is a lot easier to sustain with a team that already knows your industry, your margins, and your tax picture. Kinexus CPAs works with contractors, restaurant operators, real estate investors, medical practices, and service-based businesses across St. George on exactly this kind of month-to-month financial discipline, backed by CFO-level business management services and a modern, secure digital process for the paperwork behind it.

Schedule a consultation with the Kinexus CPAs team and start building a budget that holds up against rising costs instead of falling behind them.

### Upskilling your workforce a smart strategy for overcoming labor market shortages
URL: /upskilling-your-workforce-a-smart-strategy-for-overcoming-labor-market-shortages

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: st-george-business-owner-hiring.jpg | alt: "St George business owner reviewing staffing schedule in office" | query: "small business owner staffing schedule office" -->
## Why labor shortages are hitting St George businesses hard

Washington County's population growth has been good for business and brutal for hiring. Contractors in St George are competing with Las Vegas and Salt Lake wages for the same pool of skilled framers and electricians. Restaurant owners along St George Boulevard are running short-staffed on weekend shifts. Medical practices in the Dixie Regional corridor are waiting months to fill front-desk and clinical support roles.

Every open position costs money whether it's filled or not. Overtime climbs, service slows, quality slips, and owners end up doing the work of three people instead of running the business. A construction crew missing two skilled workers can push a project timeline by weeks. A restaurant short two line cooks turns away covers on a Friday night. The math is the same across industries: unfilled roles are a direct hit to revenue, not just an HR headache.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: employee-training-session-workplace.jpg | alt: "Manager training an employee on new equipment in a workplace setting" | query: "manager training employee workplace" -->
## The real cost of hiring new staff versus training the team you have

Recruiting a new employee typically runs 20 to 30 percent of that role's annual salary once you account for job postings, interview time, onboarding, and the productivity dip while they ramp up. For a $50,000 position, that's $10,000 to $15,000 before the new hire has produced a single billable hour or completed job.

Training an existing employee into a higher-skill role costs a fraction of that, and you're building on someone who already knows your processes, your customers, and your standards. A restaurant that cross-trains a server into a shift lead avoids an external management search entirely. A construction firm that pays for a foreman's OSHA 30 certification gets a more capable jobsite supervisor without a six-week vacancy.

This is a financial decision as much as an operational one. Shawn T. Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc, and the team at Kinexus work with St George business owners to model both paths against actual payroll and revenue numbers, not general industry averages, before recommending which one makes sense.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: tax-documents-calculator-desk.jpg | alt: "Tax documents and calculator on a desk representing business tax credits" | query: "tax documents calculator business desk" -->
## Tax incentives and credits that make training more affordable

Training budgets go further when they're structured with tax strategy in mind. Several federal and state provisions can offset the cost of upskilling employees, and most business owners never claim them because no one flagged the opportunity during tax prep.

- Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC) for hiring and training individuals from targeted groups
- Section 162 deductions for ordinary and necessary training and education expenses
- Utah workforce development incentives tied to industry-specific training partnerships
- Employer-provided educational assistance programs under Section 127, up to $5,250 per employee tax-free
- Apprenticeship and certification reimbursement structured to maximize deductibility

A year-round tax planning relationship, rather than a once-a-year filing appointment, is what catches these before December 31. Peter Williams, EA, MAcc, and Andrew (Andy) James Stewart, EA, regularly review training and hiring plans mid-year with clients specifically to identify credits like these before the window closes.

<!-- block: industry-cards | variant: 3-col -->
## Building an upskilling plan for your industry

A generic training budget rarely produces a return. The skills worth investing in look different depending on what you build, serve, or provide.

### Construction
icon: Hammer

Cross-train laborers into equipment operators, invest in OSHA and safety certifications, and develop a project superintendent from within instead of recruiting one externally. Pairing this with accurate WIP schedules helps you see whether a trained crew is actually improving job margins.

### Restaurants
icon: Wrench

Move line cooks toward sous chef responsibilities, train servers into shift leads, and formalize food safety certifications across the team. Multi-location operators can standardize this training once and apply it at every site.

### Medical practices
icon: Stethoscope

Certify medical assistants for expanded clinical duties, train front-office staff in billing and coding accuracy, and reduce reliance on costly locum or temp-agency staffing by building depth on your existing team.

### Service-based businesses
icon: Users

Consultants, agencies, and staffing firms grow fastest when senior staff train junior hires into billable roles faster. Formal mentorship structures and certification reimbursement cut ramp-up time and improve utilization rates.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: advisor-reviewing-budget-with-client.jpg | alt: "Financial advisor reviewing budget projections with a business client" | query: "financial advisor reviewing budget client meeting" -->
## How proactive financial planning supports workforce investment

Upskilling only pays off if you can measure it. That means budgeting training costs against expected productivity gains, tracking whether the investment actually reduced turnover or overtime, and adjusting the plan before it drains cash flow.

This is where CFO-level insight matters more than a spreadsheet. RJ Mathews, CPA, and Chase Gubler, CPA, MAcc, work with clients throughout the year to build training costs into cash flow forecasts and quarterly reviews, not just the annual budget. Morgan Nethercott, CPA, brings the same discipline to entity-level financial statements so owners can see, industry by industry, whether a training dollar spent on a construction foreman or a restaurant shift lead is actually showing up in the numbers three months later.

A modern, secure digital process for document handling means this data is available in real time, not buried in a shoebox of receipts at tax season.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: consultation-handshake-office.jpg | alt: "Business owner and advisor shaking hands after a consultation meeting" | query: "business advisor client handshake meeting" -->
## Get a workforce and tax strategy built for your business

Labor shortages aren't going away, and neither is the cost of guessing at your training budget. Kinexus CPAs & Advisors works with construction firms, restaurants, medical practices, and service-based businesses across St George to connect workforce decisions to tax credits, cash flow, and long-term growth planning.

Schedule a consultation to talk through your hiring plans, what credits you might be leaving on the table, and how to budget training investment without guessing at the payoff.

## Tax planning tips for growing businesses

Multi-entity structures, high-income years, and asset sales all change the math on what you owe. These tips come from work our CPAs, including Shawn T. Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc, do year-round with business owners deciding how to structure, sell, or grow.

### Choosing the right entity before year-end
photo: entity-structure-review.jpg
query: business owner reviewing legal documents

### What related-entity transactions mean for your tax bill
photo: related-entity-transactions.jpg
query: two business owners discussing contract

If you run more than one business, or lease property to your own company, the IRS expects those transactions to be priced like they'd be between strangers. Get this wrong and an audit gets expensive fast.

### Knowing your business's real value before you need it

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: bookkeeping-systems-review.jpg | alt: "Small business owner organizing receipts and invoices at a desk" | query: "small business owner organizing paperwork" -->
## Bookkeeping and back-office tips for small business owners

Most owners start out doing their own books, and most outgrow it faster than they realize. These tips mark the point where spreadsheets stop being enough.

- Reconcile bank accounts monthly, not quarterly. Errors compound the longer they sit.
- Separate business and personal accounts on day one, not after your first tax season.
- Move to zero-based budgeting when inflation makes last year's budget meaningless. [See how it works](/zero-based-budgeting-a-smarter-way-to-manage-your-money-during-persistent-inflation)
- Track job costs or project margins in real time, not at year-end, if you bid or quote work.
- Know the difference between bookkeeping and outsourced accounting before you outgrow a part-time hire. Our [bookkeeping](/what-we-do/bookkeeping) and [outsourced accounting](/what-we-do/outsourced-accounting) services pick up exactly where DIY stops working.

### Refund tracker
URL: /resources/refund-tracker

<!-- block: intro-text | variant: centered -->
## Check your refund status in seconds

You don't need an account, a password, or a phone call to find out where your refund stands. Below are direct links to the official IRS and Utah State Tax Commission tools, so you can check in under a minute, no login required. We built this page because clients ask us this question every February through April, and the fastest answer is the government site itself, not a guess from us. Kinexus CPAs files returns correctly the first time, which cuts down on delays before they start. Once a return is submitted, though, tracking it sits with the IRS or the state, not with your preparer. These links get you the same status information their own phone reps see.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image | image: federal-refund-tracking.jpg | alt: "Person checking federal tax refund status on a laptop at home" | query: "person checking laptop tax refund" -->
## Federal refund tracking links

The IRS updates refund status once every 24 hours, usually overnight, so refreshing the page five times before lunch won't turn up anything new. E-filed returns typically show a status within 24 hours of acceptance. Paper returns can take four weeks or longer before anything appears at all. Before you click through, have your Social Security number, filing status, and exact refund amount ready. The tool requires all three to pull up your record.

- [IRS Where's My Refund](https://www.irs.gov/refunds), check the status of your current-year federal refund directly through the IRS.
- [Where's My Amended Return](https://www.irs.gov/filing/wheres-my-amended-return), track a Form 1040-X after you've filed an amendment. These can take up to 16 weeks to fully process.

<!-- block: checklist-section | variant: with-image-left | image: utah-state-refund-tracking.jpg | alt: "Utah taxpayer reviewing state tax refund status on a phone" | query: "person reviewing tax documents phone" -->
## Utah state refund tracking links

Utah processes refunds through its Taxpayer Access Point, and the timeline runs separately from the IRS. E-filed Utah returns generally move through the system within a few weeks. Paper filings take longer, since they're reviewed by hand rather than scanned automatically. Utah's status codes also differ from the federal tool's, so don't assume a mismatch between your state and federal status means something went wrong. It usually just means the two agencies are on different clocks.

- [Utah TAP Where's My Refund](https://tax.utah.gov/online-services/wheres-my-refund/), look up your Utah state refund status directly through the Utah State Tax Commission.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-right | image: irs-notice-review.jpg | alt: "Tax professional reviewing an IRS notice letter with a client" | query: "accountant reviewing letter with client" -->
## What to do if your refund is delayed or flagged

A refund that's stuck usually comes down to one of three things: identity verification, a math-error notice, or a manual review flag. The IRS sends a letter in each case, and what you do with it matters more than most people realize. Respond the wrong way, or ignore it, and your refund can sit for months instead of weeks. Andrew (Andy) James Stewart, EA, and Peter Williams, EA, handle IRS correspondence for Kinexus clients on a regular basis, drafting responses to notices, walking through identity verification through the correct channel, and following up with the IRS directly rather than leaving it to a client to sit on hold. If a notice landed in your mailbox and the language reads like legal code, that's exactly the situation our audit protection service was built for. You shouldn't have to decode an IRS letter alone to find out what's happening with your own money.

<!-- block: content-split | variant: image-left | image: tax-planning-meeting.jpg | alt: "CPA discussing tax planning strategy with a business owner at a desk" | query: "cpa meeting business owner planning" -->
## Get proactive tax planning so refunds aren't a surprise

A big refund feels good, but it usually means you gave the IRS an interest-free loan on your own money for twelve months. A surprise bill is worse: it means your withholding or estimated payments were off, and now you're scrambling to cover it in April. Both are signs nobody looked at your numbers between filing seasons. Shawn T. Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc, and the Kinexus team build tax plans in spring and fall, not just the two weeks before the deadline, adjusting withholding, timing income and deductions, and flagging opportunities before December 31 instead of after. If your refund (or your bill) keeps catching you off guard, that's not bad luck. That's a planning gap, and it's fixable before next filing season starts.

<!-- block: cta-banner | variant: image-bg | image: st-george-cpa-consultation.jpg | alt: "CPA advisor shaking hands with a client in a modern office" | query: "advisor handshake client office" -->
## Talk to a local CPA about your return

Tracking a refund tells you where things stand today. A conversation with a CPA tells you how to get a better result next year, whether that means cleaner bookkeeping, a smarter entity structure, or a tax plan that keeps more of your money working for you instead of sitting with the IRS. Kinexus CPAs works with contractors, restaurant owners, real estate investors, medical practices, and service-based businesses across St. George and southern Utah on exactly this kind of planning, backed by a team of CPAs, EAs, and MAcc-credentialed advisors. [Schedule a consultation](/contact) and let's look at your return together.
