## Resources

### Could Your Construction Innovation Qualify for the R&D Tax Credit?
URL: /resources/could-your-construction-innovation-qualify-for-the-r-d-tax-c

Most contractors we meet are profitable on paper and have never once asked whether their problem-solving counts as research. It usually does not occur to them. A framer spends three weeks working out why a wall assembly fails a moisture test in a 105-degree Washington County summer, tries four fixes, and moves on to the next job. The solution is built into the house, and the time is buried in labor cost. For some of those projects, that work is exactly what the federal research credit was written to reward.

The R&D tax credit for construction companies is real, it is underused, and it fails or succeeds on paperwork. Here is how the test works, what you need to keep, and how the rules look after the 2025 tax law changes.

## Why contractors assume the research credit is not for them

The credit lives in Section 41 of the tax code, and the name sounds like a lab coat and a patent filing. In practice, the statute does not care what industry you are in. It cares about what your team did on a specific business component, such as a product, process, technique, or design.

For a builder, that business component might be a panelized wall system, a foundation design for a hillside lot, a new method for installing radiant barriers in an attic, or a prefabrication workflow that changes how you frame. Routine work built to a known plan does not qualify. Developing a new or improved approach, where the answer was not known when you started, can.

The credit is also not a deduction. A deduction lowers taxable income. A credit lowers your tax bill dollar for dollar, which is why even a modest claim gets a CPA's attention.

## Where the four-part test meets a St George job site

Every qualified activity has to pass all four parts of the test. The IRS describes the credit mechanics on its [About Form 6765 page](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-6765), and the four parts are worth walking through with a construction example.

Say a custom home builder in St George wants to cut cooling loads in a desert climate. Their idea is a site-assembled wall panel with a ventilated cavity and a reflective layer, finished in standard stucco.

| Test | What it requires | How the example meets it |
|---|---|---|
| Permitted purpose | The work aims at a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality | The panel is meant to improve thermal performance and moisture resistance |
| Technological in nature | The work relies on engineering or physical science principles | Heat transfer, vapor diffusion, and structural loading drive the design |
| Elimination of uncertainty | You did not know at the outset the capability, method, or appropriate design | The team could not tell whether the cavity depth would dry out or trap moisture under stucco |
| Process of experimentation | You evaluated alternatives through modeling, simulation, or systematic trial and error | Three mock-up assemblies were built, instrumented, and tested before one went on a live job |

Notice what is absent: the project did not have to succeed. A failed mock-up that taught you something still counts as experimentation. What does not count is work after the design is final, cosmetic changes, or solving a problem by looking up the answer in a manufacturer's spec sheet.

The statute also has a threshold: substantially all of the activities on a business component, generally read as 80 percent or more, must be experimentation for a qualified purpose. That is why we scope claims by component rather than by whole project.

## A worked example with real numbers

This is a hypothetical, built to show the arithmetic. Our builder's wall panel effort runs over about eight months.

- **Wages:** a project manager, a lead carpenter, and two crew members spend a documented portion of their time on design, mock-ups, and testing. Qualified wages total $180,000.
- **Supplies:** lumber, membranes, sensors, and stucco for the mock-ups total $40,000. These are consumed in the research, not equipment you depreciate.
- **Contract research:** an outside structural engineer is paid $30,000 to model the assembly. Generally, 65 percent of that, or $19,500, counts.

Qualified research expenses come to $239,500. Under the alternative simplified method, the credit is 14 percent of the amount above half of your average prior three years of qualified spending. If that three-year average was $100,000, the base is $50,000, the excess is $189,500, and the credit is about $26,530. That is before any adjustment under Section 280C, where you either reduce your deduction by the credit or elect a reduced credit. We model both and pick the better one.

Utah also has its own research activities credit that builds on the federal definitions, so we check state eligibility in the same pass.

## What counts as a qualified expense

There are three buckets, and construction businesses tend to trip on the second and third.

- **Wages.** Employees doing the research, directly supervising it, or directly supporting it. The owner's time counts if the owner is doing the work and is on payroll. Time spent bidding, estimating, or managing a crew on routine work does not.
- **Supplies.** Tangible property used up in the research. Land and depreciable equipment are out. Test materials, mock-up lumber, and sensors are in.
- **Contract research.** Generally 65 percent of what you pay an outside party, such as an engineer or testing lab, to perform qualified research on your behalf. You must bear the economic risk, and you generally need to retain rights to the results.

That last point matters for contractors. If a customer funds the work and you get paid regardless of whether it succeeds, the research may be treated as funded and fall out. Fixed-price work where you absorb the risk of failure looks very different from cost-plus work, so contract terms are part of the analysis. If you build for a developer or a government agency, read the contract language before assuming anything.

## Documentation that holds up in an audit

This is where claims succeed or fail. The IRS does not need perfection, but it does expect records created while the work was happening, not a narrative assembled two years later.

What we ask construction clients to keep:

1. **Project files.** Design sketches, engineering calculations, RFIs, and change-order notes that show the uncertainty you faced.
2. **Test records.** Photos of mock-ups, moisture readings, blower-door results, and notes on what failed and why.
3. **Time tracking.** Hours by employee, by project, and by activity. A weekly code in your timekeeping system is far stronger than a year-end estimate.
4. **Payments.** Invoices from engineers and testing labs, with scope descriptions that match the research.
5. **A short project summary.** One page per business component stating the goal, the uncertainty, the alternatives tried, and the outcome.

This is easier when your books are already organized by job. If your job costing is solid, adding a research flag to a cost code costs almost nothing. If it is not, [construction accounting](/who-we-serve/construction) is the place to start before any credit study. Peter Williams (EA, MAcc) works with contractors on exactly this kind of job-level structure, and Shawn Gubler (CPA, CTC, MAcc) brings the advanced tax planning side.

A well-documented claim is also easier to defend. If the IRS sends questions, [audit protection](/what-we-do/audit-protection) means someone on our team handles the response rather than you.

## How Section 174 changes the math

Section 174 is the companion rule that determines how research costs are deducted. For tax years beginning in 2022 through 2024, businesses had to capitalize domestic research and experimental costs and amortize them over five years. That hurt cash flow even for companies that never claimed a credit, because wages for engineers and developers could no longer be deducted in full in the year paid.

The 2025 tax law (OBBBA) added Section 174A, which restores immediate expensing of domestic research costs for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024. Smaller businesses, generally those with average gross receipts of $31 million or less, may be able to apply the change retroactively to 2022 through 2024, subject to election deadlines. Foreign research is still amortized over 15 years.

Why this matters to a contractor: the credit and the deduction interact. Claiming the credit means adjusting your deduction or taking the reduced credit. Depending on your history, going back to amend earlier years may produce a refund. Whether that is worth the effort depends on your numbers, and we run it both ways before recommending anything. Our [business tax planning](/what-we-do/business-tax) work covers that modeling year-round, not just in March.

## The payroll tax offset for newer companies

A smaller group of readers can use the credit before they owe any income tax. A qualified small business, generally one with under $5 million in gross receipts and no receipts more than five years back, can elect to apply up to $500,000 of the credit against payroll taxes. Up to $250,000 offsets the employer share of Social Security tax, and up to $250,000 offsets the employer Medicare share.

The election is made on Form 6765 with a timely filed return, and the offset is taken on Form 8974 against quarterly payroll filings. For a young St George contractor or design-build startup with a heavy payroll and little taxable income, that turns a credit that would otherwise carry forward into cash. Most established contractors will not qualify on the five-year test, but a company that spun out a new entity to develop a product line might.

## Common Questions

**Does a general contractor qualify for the R&D tax credit?**

Yes, if the work meets the four-part test. A general contractor developing a new building method, assembly, or process can qualify, while routine construction to a standard plan does not. The claim is built around specific business components, such as a prefab system, and the hours spent experimenting on them.

**How far back can we claim the credit?**

You can generally amend returns for the prior three years, and unused credits carry forward 20 years. Because documentation drives the claim, older years are only worth pursuing if records from that time survive. We review what you have before estimating any refund.

**Is the credit worth it for a small contractor?**

It can be. In the example above, a $239,500 effort produced roughly $26,500 in credit. The cost-benefit depends on documentation quality and study fees. A smaller claim with clean records is often a better bet than a large one assembled from memory.

## Find out whether your work qualifies

If you have developed a new building method, built test mock-ups, or paid an engineer to solve a problem the plans did not answer, bring us the project files and we will tell you honestly whether a credit study makes sense. Start a conversation on our [contact page](/contact) and we will review your last two years of projects with you.

### The Construction Owner's Deadline: Why Equipment Bought After December 31 Costs You Real Money
URL: /resources/the-construction-owners-deadline-why-equipment-purchases-mad

A St. George excavation contractor we talked with this fall had a skid steer on order since October, paid in full, invoice dated December 28. It didn't roll off the dealer's lot and start moving dirt until January 6. That eight-day gap pushed a $65,000 deduction into a tax year he hadn't planned for, and it cost him real cash the following April. This happens to contractors almost every year, and the mistake is always the same: assuming the date you write the check is the date that counts. It isn't. The IRS cares about when equipment is placed in service, not when you paid for it, and that one distinction is the most avoidable tax leak we see across construction clients in Washington County.

If you run a framing crew, an excavation outfit, an HVAC install business, or a general contracting company bidding commercial jobs from St. George to Cedar City, your equipment purchases are lumpy, expensive, and highly sensitive to timing. A single decision in December can shift tens of thousands of dollars of deduction from one tax year to the next, and that shift matters more than most owners realize until it's too late to fix.

## The date that matters isn't the invoice date

For depreciation purposes, the IRS defines "placed in service" as the date property is ready and available for its assigned function, not the date you ordered it, paid a deposit, or even took title. [IRS Publication 946](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p946) lays this out directly: a truck sitting in your yard still wrapped in plastic on December 31 doesn't count. A skid steer that arrived in November but wasn't operational until a hydraulic fitting got replaced in January doesn't count either, at least not for the year you wanted it to.

This rule catches contractors every year for a simple reason: equipment lead times are unpredictable. Dealers quote four weeks and deliver in nine. A specialty attachment gets backordered. A truck needs upfitting before it can go to work. If you're planning to use a large purchase to offset a strong income year, the placed-in-service date is the only date that matters, and it needs to happen on or before December 31 of that tax year, not sometime in the pipeline.

## Bonus depreciation is back at 100 percent, but the deadline discipline still matters

For several years, contractors were racing a shrinking window. Bonus depreciation dropped from 100 percent to 80 percent in 2023, then 60 percent in 2024, then was scheduled to fall to 40 percent for 2025 equipment. Every December brought a real financial reason to buy before the percentage dropped again.

That phase-down has been reversed. Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, qualified property acquired and placed in service after January 19, 2025, qualifies for 100 percent bonus depreciation again, and the law makes it permanent rather than another temporary window. That's good news for equipment-heavy contractors, but it doesn't remove the timing pressure, it just changes what you're managing. The deduction is now bigger and more stable, but you still have to hit the placed-in-service deadline to claim it in the year you need it. A contractor with a strong 2025 income year and a truck that doesn't get placed in service until February 2026 still loses the deduction for the year that actually needed it.

There's a second layer worth planning around too. One hundred percent bonus depreciation isn't always the right move even when you qualify. If you're a growing contracting business projecting a much higher income year in 2026 or 2027, taking the full deduction now might waste it against income that was already low, when spreading depreciation, or electing out of bonus depreciation for a specific asset class, would offset higher future tax brackets more effectively. This is exactly the kind of decision that belongs in a projection conversation before year-end, not a guess made at the equipment dealer's counter.

## Section 179 versus bonus depreciation for contractors

Section 179 and bonus depreciation both let you deduct the full cost of qualifying equipment in the year it's placed in service, but they work differently, and the differences matter for how you sequence purchases.

| | Section 179 | Bonus depreciation |
|---|---|---|
| 2025 limit | $2,500,000 | No dollar cap |
| Phase-out | Begins once total equipment purchases exceed $4,000,000 | None |
| Taxable income limit | Deduction can't exceed business taxable income | No income limitation |
| New or used property | Both qualify | Both qualify |
| Carryforward | Unused deduction carries forward | Not applicable, no income limit to hit |

For most St. George contractors, the taxable income limitation on Section 179 is the detail that trips people up. If your business shows a loss or thin profit in a slow year, a large Section 179 election can't create or deepen that loss the way bonus depreciation can. Bonus depreciation has no income ceiling, which makes it the more flexible tool when you're buying heavy equipment in a year where net income is uncertain until the books close.

Vehicle rules add another wrinkle. Pickup trucks and work trucks with a gross vehicle weight rating over 6,000 pounds, which describes most contractor trucks and heavy-duty crew cabs, qualify for both Section 179 and bonus depreciation without the passenger-vehicle luxury caps that apply to lighter vehicles. If your fleet plan includes a new dump truck or a loaded crew cab, that weight threshold is worth confirming with your CPA before you sign the purchase order, not after.

## The 179D deduction for contractors building energy efficient commercial space

Most equipment-focused tax planning stops at trucks and machinery, but contractors doing commercial design-build work have another deduction worth knowing about. The [Energy Efficient Commercial Buildings Deduction](https://www.irs.gov/credits-deductions/energy-efficient-commercial-buildings-deduction), known as Section 179D, rewards efficiency improvements to lighting, HVAC, and building envelope systems in commercial buildings.

This one matters most for general contractors and design-build firms working on government-owned or tax-exempt buildings, such as school districts, municipal buildings, or public facilities anywhere in Washington County. Because tax-exempt entities can't use a deduction themselves, the building owner can allocate the 179D deduction to the designer or contractor responsible for the energy-efficient systems. If your firm has bid public work involving lighting retrofits, upgraded HVAC, or building envelope improvements, it's worth confirming whether that allocation was ever claimed. It's frequently left on the table simply because nobody asked.

## Buy, finance, or lease changes your cash flow math

A deduction is only useful if it lines up with cash you actually have. Contractors on cash-basis accounting sometimes buy equipment specifically to reduce a tax bill, without checking whether the purchase drains working capital right when payroll or a subcontractor payment is due.

Financing the purchase, rather than paying cash, often solves this. You can still take the full Section 179 or bonus depreciation deduction on financed equipment, even though you're only making a down payment and monthly note, which means you get the full tax benefit in the current year while spreading the actual cash outlay over 36 or 60 months. Leasing is a different animal entirely: true operating leases don't generate a depreciation deduction at all, since you don't own the asset, though the lease payment itself is deductible as an ordinary expense. For a contractor deciding between a $180,000 excavator purchase and a lease, the right answer depends on projected income, existing debt service, and how long you plan to keep the machine, not just which option has the lower monthly payment.

This is where entity structure comes into play too. Contractors running multiple entities, an operating company and an equipment-holding company, for example, need the purchase and the placed-in-service documentation to sit with the entity that actually generates the income you're trying to offset. Get that mismatched, and the deduction can end up stranded in an entity with no income to absorb it.

## A Q4 checklist built around your actual numbers

Waiting until the last week of December to think about equipment is how contractors end up buying the wrong thing at the wrong time for the wrong reason. A better sequence looks like this:

- **Run a real income projection by mid-October.** You need to know your actual taxable income trajectory before deciding how much deduction you need, not guess based on last year's return.
- **Confirm delivery and placed-in-service timing with the dealer in writing.** Verbal promises about "before year-end" delivery are not documentation the IRS will accept if the equipment arrives late.
- **Photograph and log the in-service date.** A dated photo of the machine on your jobsite, plus the operator log showing first use, is simple proof that holds up if the deduction is ever questioned.
- **Decide on financing structure before the purchase, not after.** Once the note is signed, restructuring for cash flow reasons gets harder.
- **Match the purchase to the right entity.** If you operate under a WIP schedule and percentage-of-completion accounting, your [WIP schedule](/industries/construction/wip-schedules-percentage-completion) already reflects which entity is carrying the income; the equipment deduction should follow it.

Our construction clients, from framing crews to commercial general contractors around St. George, get this analysis done as part of the quarterly projection process our team runs year-round, not as a scramble during the last week of the year. Peter Williams, EA, MAcc, works with contractor clients specifically on this kind of equipment and WIP-schedule coordination, and Shawn T. Gubler, CPA, CTC, MAcc, brings Certified Tax Coach-level strategy to owners weighing bonus depreciation against multi-year income projections. That's the difference between [proactive business tax planning](/what-we-do/business-tax) and a once-a-year filing exercise.

## Common mistakes we see every December

A few patterns show up in almost every contractor's file when equipment planning happens too late:

- Buying equipment based on a tax bill estimate that was never actually run against year-to-date books.
- Taking full bonus depreciation in a low-income year, then having nothing left to offset a much bigger income year that follows.
- Purchasing under a personal name or the wrong entity, then trying to fix the ownership after the fact.
- Assuming a deposit or purchase order counts as "placed in service," then losing the deduction when delivery slips past December 31.
- Skipping the projection conversation entirely and finding out about the deduction limits during tax prep, when the only options left are the ones already locked in.

Every one of these is fixable with a conversation in October or November. None of them are fixable in April.

Equipment planning is one piece of a bigger picture for contractors, and it connects directly to entity structure, WIP accounting, and the advanced tax strategy work covered in our [advanced tax planning services](/services/advanced-tax-planning) for owners in higher income brackets. If your business is bidding bigger jobs, adding a second entity, or looking at a major equipment purchase before year-end, that's exactly the kind of decision worth reviewing with someone who works construction numbers, not general small business numbers, on our [construction accounting](/who-we-serve/construction) team.

## Common Questions

**Does a deposit or down payment on equipment count as placed in service?**
No. A deposit only secures the purchase; the deduction depends on the equipment being delivered, assembled, and ready for its intended use in your business. If a truck or excavator doesn't reach that point until January, the deduction moves to next year regardless of when you paid for it.

**Is bonus depreciation still worth using now that it's back to 100 percent?**
Usually yes, but not automatically. If your income is unusually low this year and expected to jump significantly next year, taking 100 percent bonus depreciation now can waste the deduction against income that didn't need it. A projection comparing this year and next is the only way to know for sure.

**Can I still use Section 179 if my business had a loss this year?**
Section 179 can't create or increase a business loss, since it's capped at your taxable income for the year. Bonus depreciation has no such limit, so it's often the better tool in a year where profit is thin or uncertain.

**What documentation do I need to prove an equipment purchase was placed in service by December 31?**
A dated delivery receipt, a photo of the equipment on the jobsite, and an operator or usage log showing first use are the strongest combination. Verbal assurances from a dealer about delivery timing are not enough if the IRS ever asks for proof.

If you're weighing an equipment purchase before year-end, or you simply don't know whether this year's income can absorb the deduction you're planning on, get that answered before you sign anything. Reach out through our [contact page](/contact) and we'll run the numbers with you.

### OBBBA's Expanded Home Construction Exception: What It Means for Builders
URL: /resources/obbbas-expanded-home-construction-exception-why-builders-sho

If you build homes or develop residential lots in Washington County, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act just changed a rule that's been forcing builders into complicated tax accounting for decades. The home-construction exception to the percentage-of-completion method under IRC Section 460 has been expanded, and for contracts entered into after the law's enactment, more residential projects will qualify to skip percentage-of-completion entirely. That's a real opportunity for cash flow and tax timing, but only if you plan the method change before your 2026 contracts start locking you in.

This isn't a rule change you want to discover during tax season. Builders who wait until their CPA is preparing the 2026 return will have already signed contracts under the old assumptions, missed elections, and possibly locked themselves into percentage-of-completion for jobs that didn't need to be there.

## What the home construction exception actually does

Under Section 460, most long-term contracts, meaning contracts not completed within the tax year they're started, have to use the percentage-of-completion method (PCM). PCM requires builders to recognize revenue and pay tax on income as a project progresses, based on costs incurred versus total estimated costs. That's fine for a commercial general contractor with steady cash draws. It's brutal for a homebuilder sitting on unsold spec inventory or waiting on a buyer's financing to close, because it can create a tax bill before the cash from the sale ever shows up.

The home construction exception has always let contracts meeting certain criteria, primarily that 80% or more of estimated costs relate to dwelling units in buildings with four or fewer units, use the completed contract method or another exempt method instead. Under the completed contract method, income and expenses aren't recognized until the project is substantially complete. For a builder financing land and construction costs out of pocket for 12 to 18 months before closing, that deferral can be the difference between a normal tax year and a cash crunch.

OBBBA widens who fits inside that exception. More residential projects, including certain multi-unit developments and projects that previously fell just outside the old thresholds, now qualify. The practical effect: builders who've been stuck using PCM because of a technicality in their old contracts may be able to shift eligible new contracts to completed contract accounting starting with agreements signed after the law took effect.

## Why the 2026 contract date matters

The expanded exception applies to contracts entered into after enactment. For a calendar-year taxpayer, that means contracts signed in 2026 are squarely within the new rules, while contracts already in progress from 2024 or 2025 are generally stuck with whatever method applied when they were signed. That creates a clear planning window right now, not later.

Here's the trap: if a builder in St. George signs a batch of new home contracts in January 2026 without revisiting their accounting method election, they may default into the same PCM treatment they've used for years, simply because nobody flagged that the contracts now qualify for an exemption. Method elections aren't automatic. They require an affirmative decision, and in some cases an IRS method change filing, to apply the new treatment correctly and consistently.

## Method changes take more than a checkbox

Switching between percentage-of-completion and completed contract accounting is a change in accounting method, not just a different way of filling out a form. That generally means a Form 3115 filing, an analysis of any Section 481(a) adjustment, and a decision about whether the change applies only to new contracts or requires broader consistency across a builder's existing contract portfolio.

There's also the look-back method to consider. Contracts that stay on percentage-of-completion, or that were on PCM before shifting exempt status, may be subject to look-back interest calculations under the rules covered in the [IRS Instructions for Form 8697](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i8697). Builders who assume the new exception wipes out all prior look-back exposure are often wrong, and that's a costly assumption to make without checking.

## Who benefits most from the expanded exception

The builders who stand to gain the most from this change share a few traits:

| Builder profile | Why the exception helps |
|---|---|
| Spec home builders carrying unsold inventory | Defers income recognition until sale closes, not while units sit unsold |
| Small multi-unit developers (duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes) | Newly qualifying project types can move off PCM |
| Builders with long closing cycles due to buyer financing delays | Matches tax liability to actual cash receipt |
| Contractors mixing residential and light commercial work | Need contract-by-contract analysis to apply the exception correctly |

Builders working exclusively on custom homes under contract with a buyer from day one, where the home is essentially pre-sold, may see less benefit since income timing was already closer to cash timing. The exception matters most where there's a real gap between when costs are incurred and when cash from the sale arrives.

## What St. George builders should do before signing 2026 contracts

Start with a contract-level review, not a blanket policy change. Every job needs to be checked against the 80% cost threshold and unit-count rules to confirm it actually qualifies for the exception. Then decide, with your CPA, whether completed contract accounting genuinely improves your position, since deferring income also means deferring the ability to use losses or credits in the year costs are incurred. For builders with tight financing covenants tied to reported income, PCM may still be the better call even where the exemption is available.

We've walked contractors through WIP schedule rebuilds before, and the same discipline applies here: know your numbers by contract, not just in aggregate. Our team already prepares [WIP schedules and percentage of completion accounting](/industries/construction/wip-schedules-percentage-completion) for builders across the region, and this law change is exactly the kind of shift that needs to run through that same job-costing detail before a method election gets filed.

If your business also carries retainage balances or seasonal cash gaps on top of this, it's worth reading how we help contractors plan around [retainage tying up cash](/retainage-is-holding-your-cash-hostage-heres-how-to-plan-around-it), since the two issues often compound each other during long construction cycles.

## Common Questions

**Does the expanded home construction exception apply to contracts already in progress?**
Generally no. The exception applies to contracts entered into after the law's enactment date, so most 2024 and 2025 contracts stay under whatever method applied when they were signed. New contracts signed in 2026 and later are where the expanded rules take effect for calendar-year taxpayers.

**Is switching to completed contract method always better for cash flow?**
Not always. Completed contract accounting defers income recognition, which helps cash flow timing, but it also defers deductions and can affect financing covenants or bonding requirements that rely on reported income. A contract-by-contract review is the only way to know for sure.

**Do we need to file anything with the IRS to change methods?**
In most cases, yes. A change between percentage-of-completion and completed contract method is treated as an accounting method change, which typically requires a Form 3115 filing and analysis of any required adjustment. This isn't something to handle with a simple internal policy memo.

**How does this interact with the look-back method?**
Contracts that were or remain on percentage-of-completion may still trigger look-back interest calculations, detailed in the [IRS Instructions for Form 8697](https://www.irs.gov/instructions/i8697). Moving future contracts to an exempt method doesn't automatically eliminate look-back exposure on prior jobs.

If you're signing residential construction contracts for 2026 or planning your next development phase, get this reviewed before the paperwork is final. Contact us at [/contact](/contact) and we'll walk through which of your contracts actually qualify for the expanded exception and what a method change would mean for your specific tax position.
